docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents my individual subsystem board for RAS 304 (Embedded Systems). It walks through how the board was designed: its block diagram, the components chosen and why, the power budget, the schematic and the bill of materials.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Team 102 is building a modular robotic spider leg for robotics hobbyists and students: a leg made from 3D-printed parts and off-the-shelf electronics that users can buy assembled, repair themselves, and wire into their own walking robots. The leg uses a hub-and-spoke design. Preston's hub board runs the leg kinematics and sends commands over ribbon cables to each teammate's board, and each board drives one part of the leg and reports back. Each board has its own power supply; the only connection between teammates' boards is the UART communication link.

My board, Driver Nano 3, is the spoke on hub connector 3. It drives Linear Actuator B (an N20 gearmotor turning an M3 lead screw) to the position the hub asks for, using a slide potentiometer for position feedback and motor-current sensing for stall protection. It also reads an LIS3DH accelerometer to measure the leg's jerk and impulse, which it sends back to the hub. More detail on the whole project is in the Team 102 report.

docs.text:
• Linear actuator control: DRV8833 H-bridge with current limit, MCP601 current-sense amplifier, and closed-loop position from a slide potentiometer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page shows the electrical architecture of my subsystem for Team 102's Modular Spider Leg. In the team's hub-and-spoke layout, my board is the spoke on hub connector 3. It drives the leg's small linear actuator (the actuator) and measures leg motion with an accelerometer for jerk and impulse sensing (the sensor). Commands come from Preston's hub board over the ribbon cable.

The design follows the RAS 304 project requirements:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the microcontroller.
  • A 9 V barrel jack feeding a 5 V linear regulator, with a fuse and a power-status LED. (My board adds a second linear regulator, 6 V, for the motor only.)
  • A 2x4 male IDC header using the class ribbon pinout.
  • No daughter boards: every peripheral, including the accelerometer, is placed directly on this PCB.

Parts were also chosen to stay within the team's $70–80 total budget.

The block diagram shows:

  • Power levels: my own 9 V adapter → barrel jack → 1 A fuse → 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode → two linear regulators. The L7806CV (6 V) feeds only the motor driver and the 6 V actuator motor. The L7805CV (5 V) feeds the Curiosity Nano and the power LED. The Curiosity Nano's on-board regulator supplies 3.3 V to the accelerometer, the position potentiometer and the current-sense op-amp.
  • Actuator: a DFRobot FIT0577 N20 gear motor with an M3 lead screw, driven by a TI DRV8833 H-bridge. A 0.33 Ω current-sense resistor sets a 0.61 A current limit, and an MCP601 amplifier (gain 11) scales its voltage for the ADC so the PIC can detect a stall.
  • Position feedback: a Bourns slide potentiometer whose slider moves with the actuator's lead-screw nut.
  • Sensor: an ST LIS3DH 3-axis accelerometer chip on SPI, with a data-ready interrupt.
  • Debug: two debug LEDs and a debounced push button on spare GPIO.
  • Team connection: an 8-pin ribbon cable to Preston's hub board. It carries position commands in and jerk/impulse data out over UART.

docs.title: How the Block Diagram Was Structured
docs.text:
The diagram is organized left to right by supply domain (9 V → 6 V → 5 V → 3.3 V), so a reader can follow power from the wall adapter to every load, and each dashed box states its voltage, regulator and maximum current. The microcontroller sits in the middle with each peripheral (PWM, ADC, SPI, UART, digital I/O) drawn as its own white block, so every signal line shows its type, pin count and the PIC pin it uses. Actuator parts are grouped on the left and sensing parts on the right, and the ribbon connector to Preston's hub is at the bottom right, matching the team block diagram.

Since the first version, two changes came from the power budget and feedback: the motor moved from the 5 V rail to its own 6 V regulator (the 6 V motor was running under-voltage and the 5 V regulator was overheating), and an op-amp was added after the current-sense resistor because 0–0.2 V used only a small slice of the ADC range.

docs.title: Team Connection
docs.text:
My board connects to Preston's hub board (Leg Kinematics) through hub connector 3, using the class-standard 8-pin ribbon cable and a 2x4 male IDC header. Each teammate's board is powered individually; no power is shared between boards. My board runs from its own 9 V adapter, and the only connection to the hub is communication: UART TX and RX on pins 1 and 2. Pin 8 is a common ground, which carries no supply current but is needed so both boards agree on what a UART logic high and low are. No power pins are used on the ribbon.

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• Closed-loop position control: the hub sends a target position over UART. The PIC compares it with the slide-pot reading on RA1, then drives the two PWM outputs (RC2, RD0) to move the lead screw forward or back.
  • Stall and fault protection (Req. 6.1): current through the DRV8833 flows through a 0.33 Ω sense resistor on AISEN. An MCP601 amplifies that voltage by 11, and the PIC reads it on RA0 and stops the motor if the current stays high, which indicates a stall. The same resistor also sets the driver's built-in current limit at about 0.61 A (0.2 V ÷ 0.33 Ω), which keeps a motor fault within what my 1 A adapter can supply. The nFAULT pin (RB1) reports over-current or over-temperature, and the PIC then disables the driver through nSLEEP (RD1).
  • Jerk and impulse sensing: the LIS3DH data-ready interrupt (RB0) triggers an SPI read of acceleration at up to about 1.3 kHz. Jerk is found by differentiating acceleration, and impulse by integrating force (mass × acceleration) over the foot-contact time. The results are sent to the hub over UART.
  • Accelerometer soldering: the LIS3DHTR is a 3 × 3 mm LGA-16 package. Because daughter boards aren't allowed, it is soldered directly to the PCB with a stencil and hot air or reflow.
  • Speed vs. cost: a standard M3 lead screw moves 0.5 mm per turn, so the 98 RPM (60 RPM under load) FIT0577 gives about 0.5–0.8 mm/s. That is slow, but adequate for a small demonstration leg, and much cheaper than a commercial linear actuator with built-in feedback (about $80 or more).

docs.title: 1. Subsystem summary
docs.text:
Driver Nano 3 handles Linear Actuator B control and IMU sensing. It follows this loop from the team software flow diagram:

  1. Receive the actuator B target position from the Main Processor (Preston's hub board).
  2. Drive Linear Actuator B (PWM and direction).
  3. Read the IMU orientation (SPI).
  4. Check whether the orientation is within the expected range. If yes, continue the motion. If no, adjust the motion or flag a status.
  5. Send actuator B status and IMU data back to the Main Processor.
  6. Loop, waiting for the next command.

When the Main Processor sends a stop command, Driver Nano 3 disables the driver and reports a safe status. The Main Processor does the kinematics; my board only runs local control and returns feedback continuously. The team calls the sensor output "jerk / impulse" data, which the PIC computes from the accelerometer readings.

Budget constraint: the whole team budget is $70 to $80 for four boards, so each board should cost about $17.50 to $20.00. That limits every choice below, especially the actuator.

Other project constraints:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the MCU. Its I/O and ADC run at its target voltage, 3.3 V as shipped (Curiosity Nano user guide, section 3.3.1).
  • External 9 V barrel-jack adapter, 5 V linear regulator, fuse and power indicator.
  • No daughter boards: the IMU is a bare chip on my PCB.

Choice: Option 1, DFRobot FIT0577 N20 gearmotor with M3 lead screw [Actuator B subsystem]

Rationale: The team budget is $70 to $80 for four boards, so my board has about $17.50 to $20.00 to spend in total, and the actuator must also be orderable in the US. Option 1 keeps the design from my Block Diagram page (an N20 6 V gearmotor driving an M3 lead screw) as one ready-made part, costs $9.00, and comes with published stall and no-load currents. Option 2 gives the original 300 RPM speed for a little less money, but it leaves me to buy and align the screw and coupler, and it has no published current data. The Pololu motor alone ($23.95) is more than the board's whole share, and the commercial actuator costs more than the entire team budget. I accept the slow speed (a joint demonstration does not need fast motion) and the missing feedback (covered by the slide potentiometer in 2.3). If the team needs more speed later, Option 2 is the fallback.

docs.title: 2.2 [Actuator B subsystem] Motor driver (H-bridge)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. TI DRV8833PWPR dual H-bridge, HTSSOP-16 with PowerPAD$3.02 each (Digi-Key and Mouser)Digi-Key product page · TI datasheet • MOSFET bridge: only about 0.36 Ω total on-resistance at 5 V, so about 0.2 V is lost at 0.6 A and the motor sees nearly the full 5 V• 2.7 to 10.8 V motor supply, 1.5 A RMS and 2 A peak per bridge, plenty of margin over a small N20• Adjustable current limit with one sense resistor (0.2 V ÷ R), which also gives stall detection• nFAULT output, nSLEEP pin and thermal shutdown• Logic threshold of 2 V (2.5 V on nSLEEP) works with the Nano's 3.3 V outputs• Very low sleep current• Lowest cost of the three options • Surface-mount only: 5.0 × 4.4 mm package with an exposed pad, which needs hot air or reflow to solder properly• No built-in current sense output, so an external sense resistor and ADC reading are needed• Dissipation goes through the exposed pad, so the PCB needs a copper pour under it Option 2. TI SN754410NE quadruple half-H driver, DIP-16$4.50 eachSparkFun product page · TI datasheet • Through-hole DIP, easiest to solder and replace• 1 A continuous per channel, built-in clamp diodes• Thermal shutdown • Bipolar outputs lose roughly 2.6 to 3.6 V in total near 0.6 A, so on a 5 V rail a 6 V motor would see only about 1.5 to 2.5 V and barely turn• No current limit or fault output• About 1.5 times the cost of the DRV8833• Large quiescent supply current Option 3. L293D dual H-bridge, DIP-16$8.95 each (price as listed)Adafruit product page · TI datasheet • Through-hole DIP, well documented, many examples• Internal kickback diodes • Same bipolar voltage-drop problem as Option 2, so the 6 V motor is starved on 5 V• Only 600 mA continuous, with no margin against stall• Most expensive option and no fault or current-limit features

Choice: Option 1, DRV8833PWPR [Actuator B subsystem]

Rationale: The motor is fed from the 5 V rail, so the driver must drop almost nothing. Only the MOSFET-based DRV8833 does that; the bipolar DIP drivers would waste about half of the available voltage. It is also the lowest-cost option, has a built-in current limit and fault output that give me stall detection and protection (a project requirement), and works directly from the Nano's 3.3 V signals. The cost is a harder soldering job, which I accept with a stencil and hot air or reflow, and a copper pour under the exposed pad.

docs.title: 2.3 [Actuator B subsystem] Position sensor for the lead-screw nut
docs.text:

The LIS3DH is the lowest-cost option, runs from the Nano's 3.3 V rail, supports SPI with a data-ready interrupt, and fits the budget. The other two cost at least about three to four times as much for features (gyroscope, built-in tap detection) the task does not require. The soldering risk (3 × 3 mm LGA) is accepted and handled with a stencil and hot air or reflow; this is the same risk any of the three options carries.

docs.title: 2.6 [Power subsystem] External 9 V power source
docs.text:

docs.title: 2.7 [Power subsystem] Motor supply rail (added after the power budget)
docs.text:
My first design ran the 6 V motor from the 5 V rail. The power budget showed two problems: the L7805CV would dissipate about 2.6 W and need a heatsink, and the motor would run below its rated voltage. I compared three ways to supply the motor:

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Second linear regulator, ST L7806CV (6 V, TO-220)ST L78 datasheet • Motor runs at its rated 6 V• Motor current and stall spikes stay off the microcontroller's 5 V rail• Same family, footprint and protection (current limit, thermal shutdown) as the L7805CV• Inexpensive • Needs at least 8 V in; about 8.6 V is available from the 9 V adapter after the diode• About 1.4 W of heat at stall from 9 V, more from a 12 V adapter Option 2. Keep the motor on the L7805CV 5 V rail (original design) • No extra part • L7805CV dissipates about 2.6 W and needs a heatsink• Motor runs under-voltage• Motor noise and stall dips reach the Nano's supply Option 3. Run the DRV8833 from the raw 9 V rail and cap the PWM duty near 66% • No regulator heat at all • Applies 9 V peaks to a 6 V motor• A firmware bug or reset at full duty could overdrive the motor• Supply varies with the adapter used

Choice: Option 1, L7806CV [Power subsystem]

Rationale: It is the only option that gives the motor its rated voltage while protecting the microcontroller's rail, and it adds well under a dollar. It also moved most of the heat off the L7805CV, which now needs no heatsink. See the Power Budget.

docs.title: 2.8 [Actuator B subsystem] Current-sense signal conditioning (added in the schematic)
docs.text:
The 0.33 Ω sense resistor produces only 0 to 0.2 V at the current limit. Read directly, that uses about 6% of the 3.3 V ADC range, which is too coarse for a reliable stall threshold.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Microchip MCP601-I/P op-amp, non-inverting, gain 11 (PDIP-8)Microchip MCP601 datasheet • Single-supply, rail-to-rail output, runs from the Nano's 3.3 V• 0 to 0.2 V becomes 0 to 2.2 V, using about two-thirds of the ADC range• Through-hole, easy to solder• Very low supply current (about 0.3 mA) • Adds an IC and a few resistors• Small offset error needs a zero-current calibration Option 2. Read the sense resistor directly on the ADC • No extra parts • Only about 250 ADC counts (of 4096) across the full current range• Noisy, unreliable stall threshold Option 3. Dedicated current-sense amplifier IC (for example TI INA180) • Fixed, accurate gain • Surface-mount only• Higher cost than a general op-amp• Low-side sensing here does not need its common-mode range

Choice: Option 1, MCP601-I/P [Actuator B subsystem]

Rationale: It gives the PIC a usable signal for stall detection (Requirement 6.1) with one through-hole part that runs from the existing 3.3 V rail. A 159 Hz RC filter before it and a 1.6 kHz anti-alias filter after it remove PWM ripple.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is my individual subsystem board, drawn in KiCad 10. It follows my Block Diagram, Component Selection and Power Budget pages. The board takes a position command from Preston's hub board over the ribbon cable. It drives Linear Actuator B (an N20 lead-screw gearmotor) through a DRV8833 H-bridge, closes the loop with a slide potentiometer, and reads an LIS3DH accelerometer for jerk / impulse sensing. Status and IMU data go back to the hub over UART.

  • Power: a 9–12 V barrel jack feeds a removable 1 A fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode. Two through-hole linear regulators share the C1/C2 input capacitors. The L7805CV (5 V logic rail) powers the Curiosity Nano and the green power LED. The L7806CV (6 V motor rail) powers only the DRV8833 and the N20 motor, which is rated 6 V. The Nano's on-board regulator (VTG) supplies 3.3 V to the IMU, the op-amp and the potentiometer. Only the motor and its driver run above 5 V; the raw 9–12 V reaches only the two regulator inputs.
  • Controller: the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, drawn as a custom symbol with my initials (KG). It is fed from 5 V through jumper JP1 and Schottky diode D3, so the Nano's USB 5 V cannot back-feed the board's 5 V rail. There are 0.1 µF bypass capacitors on VBUS and VTG.
  • Actuator with driver circuit: a DRV8833, powered from the 6 V rail through JP2, drives the motor from AIN1/AIN2 (RC2, RD0 PWM), with nSLEEP (RD1) and nFAULT (RB1). The 0.33 Ω sense resistor sets the chopping current limit at about 0.61 A, which stays within the 1 A adapter even in a fault. D6–D9 clamp the motor's back-EMF to VM and GND. JP2 isolates the 6 V motor rail for debugging.
  • Current-sense signal conditioning: a 159 Hz RC low-pass and an MCP601 non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 11 turn the 0–0.2 V sense voltage into 0–2.2 V for the ADC (RA0). A 1.6 kHz anti-alias filter follows the amplifier.
  • Sensor: an LIS3DHTR on SPI1 (RC3 SCK, RC4 SDI, RC5 SDO, RD4 CS), with INT1 data-ready on RB0. The slide potentiometer (off-board, on J7) is filtered and read on RA1.
  • Team interface: a 2x4 IDC header with pin 1 = UART RX (RC7) from the hub, pin 2 = UART TX (RC6) to the hub, and pin 8 = GND (signal reference only). Pins 3–7 are broken out on J3. No power passes through the ribbon: every teammate's board has its own supply, and the ribbon carries only the UART link.
  • Debug and expansion: two debug LEDs (RD2, RD3), a hardware-debounced push button (RD5), 13 bare PCB test pads, and two 13-pin spare GPIO headers that bring out every unused Nano I/O pin.

Figure 1: Driver Nano 3 subsystem schematic (click to enlarge, or open the PDF below for full resolution).

docs.title: How the Schematic Meets User Needs and Product Requirements
docs.text:
The team's users are robotics hobbyists and students who want a leg they can wire into their own robot, repair and modify (see the team's Product Requirements). This board has to move one joint on command and report how the leg is moving, safely and with parts a user can replace. The circuit does that as follows:

  • Moving the joint on command (user need: a leg that "just works" from simple commands). The hub sends a target position over UART (pin 1 of the ribbon, RC7). The PIC compares it with the slide-pot reading on RA1 and drives the DRV8833 with two PWM signals (RC2, RD0). Because the slide pot gives an absolute position, the joint knows where it is at power-up without a homing move.
  • Motor at its rated voltage. The L7806CV gives the 6 V motor its full rated voltage, while the L7805CV keeps the Curiosity Nano on a separate, quieter 5 V rail. Motor start-up and stall current cannot pull the microcontroller's supply down and reset it.
  • Stall and fault protection (Req. 6.1). The 0.33 Ω sense resistor makes the DRV8833 chop the current at about 0.61 A. The MCP601 amplifies the 0–0.2 V sense voltage to 0–2.2 V so the PIC can see a stall clearly on RA0 and stop the motor before it overheats. nFAULT (RB1) reports driver over-current or over-temperature, and D6–D9 clamp back-EMF from the motor.
  • Supply protection (Req. 6.3). A removable 1 A fuse protects against shorts, the 1N5819 protects against a reversed adapter, and both regulators have internal current limits and thermal shutdown.
  • Safe state when the controller is not running (Req. 6.4). nSLEEP has a 10k pull-down, so the motor driver is off while the PIC is in reset or being programmed. The LIS3DH chip select has a pull-up so the sensor stays idle. Firmware can drop nSLEEP if hub commands stop arriving.
  • Motion sensing for the team (jerk / impulse). The LIS3DH is on SPI1 with its data-ready interrupt on RB0, so the PIC reads each new sample as soon as it is ready and computes jerk and impulse to send back to the hub over UART (RC6).
  • Standard interfaces (Req. 2.2). UART to the hub over the class-standard 2x4 ribbon header, and SPI to the on-board accelerometer.
  • Repairable and modifiable (Req. 4.3, 4.4, 5.2). The motor (J4) and slide pot (J7) plug into headers, the fuse sits in clips, nearly every part is through-hole, and every unused Nano pin is broken out on J5 and J6. JP1 and JP2 let a user isolate the Nano or the motor rail while debugging, and the test pads, debug LEDs and button make bring-up easier.

docs.title: Budget choices
docs.text:
The team budget is $70–80 for four boards (about $17.50–20.00 per board; see Component Selection). The schematic keeps costs down where it can:

  • Test points: bare PCB pads cost nothing, instead of about $0.35 each for purchased test points.
  • Headers and jumpers: all are cut from one 40-pin break-away strip.
  • Heatsink: the L7805CV now carries only the Nano and the LED (about 0.1 A), so it needs no heatsink. Only the L7806CV, which carries the motor current, may need a small TO-220 heatsink, and only with a 12 V adapter (see the Power Budget).

New items compared with Component Selection: the L7806CV, the MCP601-I/P, the 41FR33E sense resistor (the most expensive passive) and six 1N5819 diodes, about $4–5 in total. Passives and headers should come from lab stock where possible, and the full part list is on the BOM page.

docs.title: Design checks
docs.text:
• ERC: KiCad ERC passes with 0 errors and 1 warning. The warning is the DRV8833's unused bridge-B sense pin (BISEN, bidirectional) tied to GND, where the GND PWR_FLAG sits; this is expected.
  • Capacitor voltage margin (at least 25%): 50 V ceramics on every rail; 47 µF / 25 V on 9–12 V; 10 µF / 25 V electrolytics and the 2.2 µF / 25 V VINT ceramic on 5 V and lower.
  • Test pads: TP1–TP13 are bare PCB pads, so they are not in the BOM.
  • Through-hole parts: every component is through-hole except the DRV8833PWPR (HTSSOP-16) and the LIS3DHTR (LGA-16). Neither comes in a through-hole package; both were accepted on my Component Selection page.
  • Resistor power margin (at least 50%): sense resistor 0.61² × 0.33 = 0.12 W, rated 1 W. All other resistors dissipate less than 10 mW and are rated 1/4 W.
  • Unused inputs: DRV8833 BIN1/BIN2 and the LIS3DH ADC1–3 inputs are pulled down through 10k. LIS3DH CS has a 10k pull-up and DRV8833 nSLEEP a 10k pull-down, so both stay in a safe state while the MCU is in reset.

docs.title: What the power budget showed
docs.text:
• It drove the move to a separate motor rail. The first version put the motor on the 5 V rail. The budget showed the L7805CV would dissipate about 2.6 W and needed a heatsink, and the 6 V motor would run under-voltage. Moving the motor to an L7806CV fixed both: the 5 V regulator now dissipates under 0.5 W, and the motor gets its rated 6 V.
  • It set the current-limit resistor. The original 0.2 Ω sense resistor allowed about 1 A in a motor fault, which would exceed the 1 A adapter. The budget showed a limit near 0.6 A is needed, which is why the schematic uses 0.33 Ω (0.61 A).
  • It confirmed the 9 V 1 A adapter is enough. About 326 mA remains in normal operation and about 88 mA in a fault, so no new adapter has to be bought.
  • It confirmed the 9 V minimum. The L7806CV needs about 8 V in, so the adapter must be at least 9 V after the fuse and diode.
